entry.sum: The determinant $\det A$ of a square matrix is a single number that measures how the linear map $x \mapsto Ax$ scales volume, with a sign recording whether orientation is kept or reversed. It is the unique function of the columns that is linear in each column, is zero whenever two columns are equal, and equals $1$ on the identity; the one fact to remember is that $A$ is invertible exactly when $\det A \neq 0$.
entry.why: Determinants decide invertibility in one computation, define the characteristic polynomial $\det(\lambda I-A)$ whose roots are the eigenvalues, and supply the Jacobian factor in the change-of-variables formula for multiple integrals.

links.note: The Jacobian determinant is the local volume-scaling factor in the change-of-variables formula for multiple integrals.
Signed areas and volumes, orientation, and tests for collinearity or coplanarity of points are all determinants.
The matrix-tree theorem counts spanning trees of a graph as a determinant, and Lindström–Gessel–Viennot counts non-intersecting lattice paths the same way.

blocks.body:
A square [[matrices|matrix]] $A$ either has an inverse or it does not, and Gaussian elimination will tell you which. But it would be useful to have a single number, computed from the entries, that answers the question, and that changes in a predictable way when the matrix is multiplied by another. The determinant is that number.

It also has a geometric meaning that makes all its rules natural: $|\det A|$ is the factor by which the map $x \mapsto Ax$ multiplies areas (in the plane) or volumes (in space), and the sign of $\det A$ says whether the map preserves or reverses orientation. A map that squashes space flat multiplies volume by $0$, and that is exactly the case where it cannot be undone.

blocks.title: Signed area in the plane
blocks.body:
Take a $2\times 2$ matrix with columns $u = (a, c)$ and $v = (b, d)$. The unit square is sent to the parallelogram spanned by $u$ and $v$, and its signed area is
$$\det\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix} = ad - bc.$$
For example, $u = (3, 1)$ and $v = (1, 2)$ span a parallelogram of area $3\cdot 2 - 1\cdot 1 = 5$. Swapping $u$ and $v$ gives $-5$: the same area, traversed the other way round. If $v$ is a multiple of $u$ the parallelogram is flat and $ad - bc = 0$.

Three properties of signed area pin it down completely.

1. It is linear in each column separately: stretching $u$ by a factor $t$ multiplies the area by $t$, and the area for $u + u'$ (with $v$ fixed) is the sum of the areas for $u$ and for $u'$, because the parallelograms share the base $v$ and heights add.
2. It is alternating: if the two columns are equal, the area is $0$.
3. It is normalised: the unit square has area $1$.

From 1 and 2 a fourth rule follows: swapping two columns changes the sign. Indeed, with $D$ denoting signed area,
$$0 = D(u + v, u + v) = D(u, u) + D(u, v) + D(v, u) + D(v, v) = D(u, v) + D(v, u).$$
The determinant of an $n \times n$ matrix is the function of its $n$ columns with exactly these three properties. Below we write a formula for it and then show that the three properties force that formula.

blocks.title: Determinant
blocks.body:
A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ has an inversion at each pair $i < j$ with $\sigma(i) > \sigma(j)$; its sign is $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) = (-1)^{\text{number of inversions}}$. The determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is
$$\det A = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{\sigma(i)\, i},$$
the sum over all $n!$ permutations $\sigma$ (this is the Leibniz formula).

Each term picks exactly one entry from every column and every row, multiplies them, and attaches a sign; for $n = 2$ the two terms are $a_{11}a_{22}$ and $-a_{21}a_{12}$.

blocks.title: The formula has the three properties
blocks.body:
Every term of the Leibniz formula contains exactly one entry from column $k$, so for fixed other columns $\det A$ is a linear function of column $k$: property 1. Plugging in $A = I$, only $\sigma = \mathrm{id}$ gives a nonzero product, so $\det I = 1$: property 3.

For property 2 we need one fact about permutations. Let $k < l$ and let $\sigma' = \sigma \circ (k\ l)$, the permutation with $\sigma'(k) = \sigma(l)$, $\sigma'(l) = \sigma(k)$ and $\sigma'(i) = \sigma(i)$ otherwise. Then $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma' = -\operatorname{sgn}\sigma$. Indeed, compare the inversions of the two lists $\sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(n)$ and $\sigma'(1), \dots, \sigma'(n)$. The pair of positions $(k, l)$ changes status. For each position $m$ strictly between $k$ and $l$, the two pairs $(k, m)$ and $(m, l)$ either both change status or both keep it. For a position $i$ outside that range, the pairs formed by $i$ with $k$ and with $l$ simply exchange their statuses. Pairs not involving $k$ or $l$ are untouched. So the number of inversions changes by an odd number.

If columns $k$ and $l$ of $A$ are equal, pair each $\sigma$ with $\sigma' = \sigma \circ (k\ l)$. The two products contain the same entries (one from each of the two equal columns is exchanged for the matching entry of the other), but the signs are opposite, so the terms cancel in pairs and $\det A = 0$.

Two further facts are used constantly; both follow from the Leibniz formula with a little bookkeeping.

- Transpose: $\det A^{\mathsf T} = \det A$ (a permutation and its inverse have the same number of inversions). Hence everything said about columns holds for rows too.
- Triangular matrices: if all entries below (or all above) the diagonal are $0$, then $\det A = a_{11}a_{22}\cdots a_{nn}$, because every $\sigma \ne \mathrm{id}$ uses at least one entry from the zero part.

blocks.title: Uniqueness and the product rule
blocks.body:
Let $D$ be any function of $n$ vectors in $F^n$ (here $F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$) that is linear in each argument and vanishes whenever two arguments are equal. Then for every $n\times n$ matrix $B$ with columns $b_1, \dots, b_n$,
$$D(b_1, \dots, b_n) = D(e_1, \dots, e_n)\,\det B.$$
Consequently, for all $n \times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$,
$$\det(AB) = \det A \, \det B.$$

As in the $2\times 2$ case, $D$ changes sign when two arguments are swapped. Write each column as $b_j = \sum_i b_{ij} e_i$ and expand using linearity in every argument:
$$D(b_1, \dots, b_n) = \sum_{i_1, \dots, i_n} b_{i_1 1} b_{i_2 2} \cdots b_{i_n n}\, D(e_{i_1}, \dots, e_{i_n}).$$
If two of the indices $i_1, \dots, i_n$ coincide, the term is $0$. The remaining index lists are permutations: $i_j = \sigma(j)$. Now sort the list $e_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, e_{\sigma(n)}$ into $e_1, \dots, e_n$ by repeatedly swapping two neighbours that are in the wrong order. Each such swap removes exactly one inversion and multiplies the value of $D$ by $-1$, so after as many swaps as $\sigma$ has inversions we get $D(e_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, e_{\sigma(n)}) = \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, D(e_1, \dots, e_n)$. Substituting,
$$D(b_1, \dots, b_n) = D(e_1, \dots, e_n) \sum_{\sigma} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \prod_j b_{\sigma(j)\, j} = D(e_1, \dots, e_n)\det B.$$

For the product rule, fix $A$ and set $D(b_1, \dots, b_n) = \det(Ab_1, \dots, Ab_n)$, the determinant of the matrix $AB$ (whose $j$-th column is $Ab_j$). Since $b \mapsto Ab$ is linear and $\det$ is linear in each column, $D$ is linear in each argument, and it vanishes when two arguments are equal. Also $D(e_1, \dots, e_n) = \det(Ae_1, \dots, Ae_n) = \det A$. The first part gives $\det(AB) = \det A \det B$.

blocks.title: The invertibility test
blocks.body: A square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A \neq 0$, and then $\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det A$.

If $A$ is invertible, the product rule gives $\det A \cdot \det A^{-1} = \det I = 1$, so $\det A 
eq 0$ and $\det A^{-1} = 1/\det A$.

If $A$ is not invertible, its columns are linearly dependent (see [[linear-maps]]), so some column is a combination of the others, say $a_k = \sum_{j 
e k} c_j a_j$. By linearity in column $k$, $\det A = \sum_{j
e k} c_j \det(\dots, a_j, \dots)$, where in the $j$-th term column $k$ has been replaced by $a_j$. Each of these matrices has two equal columns, so every term is $0$ and $\det A = 0$.

blocks.title: Computing determinants
blocks.body:
The Leibniz formula has $n!$ terms and is hopeless beyond $n = 4$ or so. In practice one uses the rules for row operations, which follow from the three properties (applied to rows, via $\det A^{\mathsf T} = \det A$):

- adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change $\det A$;
- swapping two rows multiplies $\det A$ by $-1$;
- multiplying a row by $t$ multiplies $\det A$ by $t$.

Gaussian elimination ([[linear-systems]]) turns any matrix into a triangular one, keeping track of these factors, and the determinant of the triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal. This takes about $n^3$ operations instead of $n!$.

For small or sparse matrices, cofactor (Laplace) expansion is convenient: for any fixed row $i$,
$$\det A = \sum_{j=1}^{n} (-1)^{i+j} a_{ij} \det A_{ij},$$
where $A_{ij}$ is $A$ with row $i$ and column $j$ deleted. It comes from grouping the Leibniz terms according to which entry of row $i$ they use; checking that the signs come out as $(-1)^{i+j}$ is a bookkeeping exercise that we omit. The signs follow a chessboard pattern starting with $+$ in the top left corner, and the same expansion works along any column.

The geometric meaning extends to all $n$: the image of the unit cube under $x \mapsto Ax$ is a parallelepiped of volume $|\det A|$, and more generally $x\mapsto Ax$ multiplies the volume of every region by $|\det A|$. The product rule then just says that scaling factors multiply when maps are composed.

blocks.title: A 3 by 3 determinant
blocks.body:
Compute $\det A$ for
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3\\ 0 & -1 & 4\\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$$
in two ways: by row reduction and by cofactor expansion.
blocks.solution:
Row reduction. Swap rows 1 and 3 to get a leading $1$ (the determinant changes sign):
$$\det A = -\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 4\\ 2 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}.$$
Subtract twice row 1 from row 3, giving row 3 $= (0, -3, 3)$, then subtract $3$ times row 2, giving $(0, 0, -9)$. Neither operation changes the determinant, and the matrix is now triangular with diagonal $1, -1, -9$. So $\det A = -(1 \cdot (-1) \cdot (-9)) = -9$.

Cofactor expansion along row 1:
$$\det A = 2\det\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 4\\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix} - 1\det\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} + 3\det\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix} = 2(-8) - (-4) + 3(1) = -9.$$
Since $\det A \ne 0$, $A$ is invertible, and $x\mapsto Ax$ multiplies volumes by $9$ while reversing orientation.

blocks.title: The Vandermonde determinant
blocks.body:
Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be numbers and let $V$ be the Vandermonde matrix whose $i$-th row is $(1, x_i, x_i^2, \dots, x_i^{n-1})$. Show that
$$\det V = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_j - x_i).$$
blocks.solution:
Induction on $n$; for $n = 1$ both sides are $1$ (the empty product). For $n \ge 2$, perform the column operations "column $k+1$ minus $x_1$ times column $k$" for $k = n-1, n-2, \dots, 1$, in that order. Each uses a column that has not yet been changed, and none changes the determinant. Entry $(i, k+1)$ becomes $x_i^{k} - x_1 x_i^{k-1} = x_i^{k-1}(x_i - x_1)$, so the new matrix has first row $(1, 0, \dots, 0)$ and, for $i \ge 2$, row $i$ equal to
$$\big(1,\ (x_i - x_1),\ x_i(x_i - x_1),\ \dots,\ x_i^{n-2}(x_i - x_1)\big).$$
Expand along the first row: only the $(1,1)$ entry survives, leaving the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix with rows $(x_i - x_1)(1, x_i, \dots, x_i^{n-2})$ for $i = 2, \dots, n$. Pulling the factor $x_i - x_1$ out of each row,
$$\det V(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{j=2}^{n} (x_j - x_1) \cdot \det V(x_2, \dots, x_n),$$
and the induction hypothesis finishes the proof.

A consequence: $\det V \ne 0$ when the $x_i$ are distinct, so for any values $y_1, \dots, y_n$ there is exactly one polynomial of degree less than $n$ with $p(x_i) = y_i$ (its coefficient vector solves $Vc = y$). For instance, with $x = (1, 2, 3)$ the determinant is $(2-1)(3-1)(3-2) = 2$.

blocks.title: A parity argument
blocks.body: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with integer entries such that every diagonal entry is odd and every off-diagonal entry is even. Prove that $A$ is invertible.
blocks.solution:
Use the Leibniz formula and work modulo $2$. The term for $\sigma = \mathrm{id}$ is $a_{11}a_{22}\cdots a_{nn}$, a product of odd numbers, hence odd. Every other permutation $\sigma$ has some $i$ with $\sigma(i) \ne i$, so its product contains the off-diagonal entry $a_{\sigma(i)\, i}$, which is even; that whole term is even. Therefore
$$\det A \equiv 1 \pmod 2,$$
so $\det A$ is an odd integer, in particular nonzero, and $A$ is invertible.

No entry needed to be computed. Since the Leibniz formula is a polynomial with integer coefficients in the entries, reducing it modulo a prime ([[congruences]]) is a standard way to show that an integer determinant is nonzero.

blocks.body:
- The determinant is not additive: $\det(A + B) \ne \det A + \det B$ in general. With $A = \operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ and $B = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$ both determinants are $0$, but $\det(A + B) = 1$.
- Scaling the whole matrix scales every row: $\det(tA) = t^n \det A$ for an $n \times n$ matrix, not $t\det A$.
- Determinants are defined only for square matrices. For a $2\times 3$ matrix $M$, $\det(M^{\mathsf T} M)$ makes sense but there is no $\det M$.
- When row reducing, remember the factors: swaps flip the sign and scaling a row scales the determinant. Only "add a multiple of another row" is free.
- The rule "diagonals down minus diagonals up" (Sarrus) works only for $3\times 3$ matrices. The analogous recipe for $4 \times 4$ matrices produces $8$ products instead of the $24$ terms of the Leibniz formula, and some of them with the wrong sign.

The determinant of $\lambda I - A$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$ whose roots are the [[eigen|eigenvalues]] of $A$. By the product rule, similar matrices $P^{-1}AP$ and $A$ have the same determinant, so the determinant belongs to the linear map, not to the basis. In several-variable calculus the factor $|\det A|$ becomes the Jacobian $|\det Df|$ in [[multiple-integrals|the change-of-variables formula]]; this is why polar coordinates bring in the factor $r$.

The product rule also says that $\det$ is a homomorphism from the group of invertible matrices to the nonzero numbers under multiplication ([[groups]]); its kernel is the special linear group. For invertible $A$, Cramer's rule ([[linear-systems]]) writes the solution of $Ax = b$ as ratios of determinants; the Vandermonde determinant explains why polynomial interpolation works ([[polynomials-roots]]); and the matrix-tree theorem counts the spanning trees of a graph as a determinant ([[graph-basics]]). Determinants are also a frequent tool among the [[linear-algebra|linear algebra methods]] for olympiad problems.

1. Compute the determinant of the $4\times 4$ matrix with $2$ on the diagonal, $1$ directly above and below the diagonal, and $0$ elsewhere.
2. Show that a real $n \times n$ matrix with $A^{\mathsf T} = -A$ has $\det A = 0$ when $n$ is odd.
3. Find the area of the triangle with vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 2)$ and $(2, 5)$ using a determinant.
4. Show that if $A$ has integer entries and $\det A = \pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ also has integer entries. (Hint: cofactors.)

checks.claim: Leibniz formula with inversion-count sign agrees with sympy det on random 4x4 integer matrices
checks.python:
import itertools, random
from sympy import Matrix
def sgn(p):
    inv = sum(1 for i in range(len(p)) for j in range(i+1,len(p)) if p[i] > p[j])
    return (-1)**inv
def leib(A):
    n = len(A); s = 0
    for p in itertools.permutations(range(n)):
        t = sgn(p)
        for i in range(n): t *= A[p[i]][i]
        s += t
    return s
for _ in range(200):
    A = [[random.randint(-9,9) for _ in range(4)] for _ in range(4)]
    assert leib(A) == Matrix(A).det()

entry.sum: An eigenvector of a square matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector $v$ that $A$ only stretches: $Av = \lambda v$ for a number $\lambda$, the eigenvalue. The eigenvalues are exactly the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\det(\lambda I - A)$ (for a real matrix, the non-real roots are its eigenvalues over $\mathbb C$), and along eigenvectors the matrix acts like plain multiplication, so powers and other functions of $A$ become easy there.
key: \lambda \text{ is an eigenvalue of } A \iff p_A(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-A)=0
entry.why: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors govern long-run behaviour: the growth rate of a linear recurrence such as Fibonacci, the stability of a linear system $x' = Ax$, the stationary distribution of a Markov chain and the vibration frequencies of a mechanical system are all read off from them.

links.note: The system $x' = Ax$ has solutions $e^{\lambda t}v$ for each eigenpair, and every solution tends to $0$ exactly when every eigenvalue has negative real part.
A stationary distribution of a Markov chain is a left eigenvector of the transition matrix for the eigenvalue $1$, and the second-largest eigenvalue modulus controls the speed of mixing.
Normal modes of vibration and the energy levels of a quantum system are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the governing linear operator.

blocks.body:
Most vectors change direction when you multiply them by a matrix. Take
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.$$
It sends $(1, 0)$ to $(2, 1)$, a different direction. But $A(1, 1) = (3, 3)$ and $A(1, -1) = (1, -1)$: along the line through $(1,1)$ the matrix simply multiplies by $3$, and along the line through $(1, -1)$ it does nothing at all. Since these two vectors form a basis, the whole map is understood: stretch by $3$ in one direction, keep the perpendicular direction fixed.

Such special directions are called eigenvectors, and the stretch factors are eigenvalues. Finding them turns a matrix, which mixes coordinates, into a list of independent one-dimensional multiplications. That is what makes questions like "what is $A^{100}$?" or "how fast does this recurrence grow?" tractable.

blocks.title: Eigenvalue and eigenvector
blocks.body:
Let $F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix with entries in $F$. A number $\lambda \in F$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ (over $F$) if there is a vector $v \in F^n$, $v \ne 0$, with
$$Av = \lambda v;$$
such a $v$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda$. The set $E_\lambda = \ker(A - \lambda I)$, consisting of all eigenvectors for $\lambda$ together with $0$, is the eigenspace of $\lambda$. A real matrix is also a complex matrix, and over $\mathbb C$ it may have additional, non-real eigenvalues (see below).

So an eigenvector spans a line that $A$ maps into itself, and the eigenvalue is the factor by which $A$ scales that line.

blocks.title: The characteristic polynomial
blocks.body:
The equation $Av = \lambda v$ can be rewritten as $(\lambda I - A)v = 0$. A nonzero solution $v$ exists exactly when $\lambda I - A$ is not invertible, which by the test in [[determinants]] means $\det(\lambda I - A) = 0$. So define the characteristic polynomial
$$p_A(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A).$$
Expanding by the Leibniz formula shows it is a polynomial of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $1$. Its roots in $F$ are the eigenvalues over $F$. The recipe is therefore:

1. compute $p_A$ and find its roots $\lambda$;
2. for each root, solve the linear system $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ by elimination; the solutions form $E_\lambda$.

For a $2\times 2$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ the characteristic polynomial is
$$\lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc) = \lambda^2 - (\operatorname{tr} A)\lambda + \det A,$$
where the trace $\operatorname{tr}A$ is the sum of the diagonal entries. For the matrix in the introduction this is $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 3)$, as expected.

Two remarks. First, the multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of $p_A$ is its algebraic multiplicity, while $\dim E_\lambda$ is its geometric multiplicity. They can differ: the shear $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has $p_A(\lambda) = (\lambda - 1)^2$, so $\lambda = 1$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$, but $E_1$ is only the line spanned by $(1, 0)$. One always has $1 \le \dim E_\lambda \le$ algebraic multiplicity; this is proved in [[diagonalization]].

Second, similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial: if $B = P^{-1}AP$ then $\lambda I - B = P^{-1}(\lambda I - A)P$, and the product rule for determinants gives $p_B = p_A$. So eigenvalues belong to the linear map, not to the choice of basis.

blocks.title: Complex eigenvalues
blocks.body:
A real matrix need not have real eigenvalues. Rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$,
$$R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix},$$
moves every nonzero vector off its own line, and indeed $p_R(\lambda) = \lambda^2 + 1$ has no real roots. Over the [[complex-numbers]] its eigenvalues are $\pm i$, with eigenvectors $(1, \mp i)$; for example $R(1, -i) = (i, 1) = i\,(1, -i)$.

This is why eigenvalue theory is most comfortable over $\mathbb C$. By the fundamental theorem of algebra, $p_A$ factors completely there,
$$p_A(\lambda) = (\lambda - \lambda_1)(\lambda - \lambda_2) \cdots (\lambda - \lambda_n),$$
with the eigenvalues listed according to algebraic multiplicity. In particular every complex square matrix has at least one eigenvector. For a real matrix the non-real eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs, since $p_A$ has real coefficients.

blocks.title: Trace and determinant from eigenvalues
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ complex matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then
$$\operatorname{tr} A = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n, \qquad \det A = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \cdots \lambda_n.$$

Compare two coefficients of $p_A(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A) = \prod_i (\lambda - \lambda_i)$, using [[polynomials-roots|Vieta's formulas]] on the right.

Constant term: put $\lambda = 0$. The left side is $\det(-A) = (-1)^n \det A$ and the right side is $\prod_i(-\lambda_i) = (-1)^n \lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_n$.

Coefficient of $\lambda^{n-1}$: on the right it is $-(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)$. On the left, expand $\det(\lambda I - A)$ by the Leibniz formula. A permutation $\sigma \ne \mathrm{id}$ moves at least two indices, so its term contains at most $n - 2$ diagonal entries $\lambda - a_{ii}$ and has degree at most $n-2$ in $\lambda$. Hence the $\lambda^{n-1}$ coefficient comes only from $(\lambda - a_{11})\cdots(\lambda - a_{nn})$, where it equals $-(a_{11} + \cdots + a_{nn}) = -\operatorname{tr} A$.

blocks.title: Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors
blocks.body: Eigenvectors $v_1, \dots, v_k$ of $A$ belonging to pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$ are linearly independent.

Suppose not, and among all nontrivial linear relations between some of the $v_i$ choose one with the fewest nonzero coefficients; after renumbering, $c_1 v_1 + \cdots + c_m v_m = 0$ with all $c_i \ne 0$. Since eigenvectors are nonzero, $m \ge 2$. Apply $A - \lambda_m I$, which sends $v_i$ to $(\lambda_i - \lambda_m)v_i$:
$$c_1(\lambda_1 - \lambda_m)v_1 + \cdots + c_{m-1}(\lambda_{m-1} - \lambda_m)v_{m-1} = 0.$$
The coefficients are nonzero because the eigenvalues are distinct, so this is a nontrivial relation with fewer terms, a contradiction.

In particular an $n\times n$ matrix with $n$ distinct eigenvalues has a basis of eigenvectors.

blocks.title: A 2 by 2 computation
blocks.body: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1\\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
blocks.solution:
Here $\operatorname{tr} A = 7$ and $\det A = 12 - 2 = 10$, so $p_A(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5)$.

For $\lambda = 5$: $A - 5I = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1\\ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$, whose kernel is spanned by $(1, 1)$. Check: $A(1,1) = (5, 5)$.

For $\lambda = 2$: $A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, whose kernel is spanned by $(1, -2)$. Check: $A(1, -2) = (2, -4)$.

As the theorem promises, $2 + 5 = 7 = \operatorname{tr} A$ and $2 \cdot 5 = 10 = \det A$, and the two eigenvectors are independent. This matrix reappears in [[diagonalization]], where these eigenvectors are used to compute $A^n$.

blocks.title: The all-ones matrix
blocks.body: Let $J$ be the $n\times n$ matrix of all ones and let $a, b$ be numbers. Find the eigenvalues of $M = aI + bJ$ and deduce $\det M$.
blocks.solution:
Let $\mathbf 1 = (1, \dots, 1)$. Every row of $J$ sums to $n$, so $J\mathbf 1 = n\mathbf 1$. If $x$ has coordinate sum $0$, then every entry of $Jx$ is that sum, so $Jx = 0$. The vectors with coordinate sum $0$ form a subspace of dimension $n - 1$ (the kernel of the nonzero linear map $x \mapsto x_1 + \cdots + x_n$, by rank–nullity).

Now $M\mathbf 1 = (a + nb)\mathbf 1$, and $Mx = ax$ whenever $x$ has coordinate sum $0$. Taking $\mathbf 1$ together with a basis of the sum-zero subspace gives $n$ independent eigenvectors ($\mathbf 1$ is not in that subspace). In that basis $M$ is diagonal with entries $a + nb, a, \dots, a$, and similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, so
$$p_M(\lambda) = (\lambda - a - nb)(\lambda - a)^{n-1}, \qquad \det M = a^{n-1}(a + nb).$$
For example, the $3\times 3$ matrix with $2$ on the diagonal and $1$ elsewhere is $I + J$, with eigenvalues $4, 1, 1$ and determinant $4$.

blocks.title: Fibonacci numbers
blocks.body: The Fibonacci numbers satisfy $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}$. Use eigenvectors of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ to find a closed formula for $F_n$.
blocks.solution:
Let $Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The recurrence says $Q(F_n, F_{n-1}) = (F_{n+1}, F_n)$, so $(F_{n+1}, F_n) = Q^n(1, 0)$.

The characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2 - \lambda - 1$, with roots $\varphi = \frac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2}$ and $\psi = \frac{1 - \sqrt 5}{2}$. Since $\lambda^2 = \lambda + 1$ for both roots, $Q(\lambda, 1) = (\lambda + 1, \lambda) = (\lambda^2, \lambda) = \lambda(\lambda, 1)$, so $(\varphi, 1)$ and $(\psi, 1)$ are eigenvectors. Because $\varphi - \psi = \sqrt 5$,
$$(1, 0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt 5}\big((\varphi, 1) - (\psi, 1)\big).$$
Applying $Q^n$ multiplies each eigenvector by the $n$-th power of its eigenvalue:
$$(F_{n+1}, F_n) = \frac{1}{\sqrt5}\big(\varphi^n(\varphi, 1) - \psi^n(\psi, 1)\big).$$
The second coordinate gives Binet's formula
$$F_n = \frac{\varphi^n - \psi^n}{\sqrt 5}.$$
Since $|\psi| < 1$, the second term tends to $0$, so $F_n$ is the integer nearest to $\varphi^n/\sqrt5$ and grows like $\varphi^n$: the dominant eigenvalue is the growth rate.

blocks.title: AB and BA
blocks.body: Let $A$ and $B$ be $n\times n$ matrices. Show that $AB$ and $BA$ have the same nonzero eigenvalues.
blocks.solution:
Let $\lambda

e 0$. Put $w = Bv$. Then $w

$$BA\,w = B(ABv) = B(\lambda v) = \lambda w,$$
so $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $BA$. Exchanging the roles of $A$ and $B$ gives the converse.

The condition $\lambda 
e 0$ was needed only to make $w$ nonzero, and for square matrices $0$ is shared too: $\det(AB) = \det A \det B = \det(BA)$, so both are singular or neither is. In fact $AB$ and $BA$ have the same characteristic polynomial (a standard fact that we do not prove here), though possibly different eigenspaces. For example with $A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ we get $AB = B 
e 0$ but $BA = 0$: the eigenspace for $0$ is a line for $AB$ and the whole plane for $BA$.

blocks.body:
- An eigenvector must be nonzero; $0$ satisfies $A0 = \lambda 0$ for every $\lambda$ and carries no information. The eigenvalue $\lambda = 0$, on the other hand, is allowed and means $A$ is singular.
- Row reduction changes eigenvalues. Eliminate only when solving $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ for an already known $\lambda$, never on $A$ itself before finding $p_A$.
- Eigenvalues do not add or multiply in general: the eigenvalues of $A + B$ or $AB$ are not obtained from those of $A$ and $B$, unless $A$ and $B$ share a basis of eigenvectors.
- $A$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ have the same eigenvalues (since $\det(\lambda I - A^{\mathsf T}) = \det(\lambda I - A)$) but usually different eigenvectors.
- A real matrix may have no real eigenvector at all, as rotations show; work over $\mathbb C$ when the characteristic polynomial does not split.

When $A$ has a basis of eigenvectors it can be written as $PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, which is [[diagonalization]]; when it does not, [[jordan|Jordan normal form]] is the replacement. For real symmetric matrices the eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular, which is [[spectral-theorem|the spectral theorem]]. The system $x' = Ax$ is solved by $e^{\lambda t}v$ for each eigenpair, the starting point of [[ode-linear]], and linear recurrences such as Fibonacci are handled the same way (compare [[generating-functions]]).

In probability, the stationary distribution of a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]] is a left eigenvector of the transition matrix (an eigenvector of its transpose) for the eigenvalue $1$. In graph theory, eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of a graph ([[graph-basics]]) count closed walks via $\operatorname{tr} A^k = \sum \lambda_i^k$. The spacing statistics of eigenvalues of large random matrices appear in [[pair-correlation]], where they are compared with the spacings between zeros of the zeta function.

entry.sum: A square matrix $A$ is diagonalisable if $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal and $P$ invertible; the columns of $P$ are then a basis of eigenvectors and the diagonal of $D$ lists the eigenvalues. In that basis $A$ just scales each coordinate, so $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$; over $\mathbb C$ the only obstruction is an eigenvalue whose eigenspace is smaller than its algebraic multiplicity.
key: A\ \text{diagonalisable over }\mathbb C\iff \dim\ker(A-\lambda I)=\text{algebraic multiplicity of }\lambda\ \text{for every eigenvalue }\lambda
entry.why: Diagonalisation turns powers, exponentials and other functions of a matrix into the same functions of numbers, which gives closed formulas for linear recurrences, explicit solutions of systems $x' = Ax$, and the long-run behaviour of Markov chains.

links.note: If $A = PDP^{-1}$, the system $x' = Ax$ decouples in the coordinates $y = P^{-1}x$ into independent equations $y_i' = \lambda_i y_i$.
Closed formulas for linear recurrences and for the number of walks of length $k$ in a graph come from diagonalising the companion or adjacency matrix.
Diagonalising a transition matrix gives its $k$-step transition probabilities and shows how fast a Markov chain approaches equilibrium.

blocks.body:
Computing $A^{100}$ for a $2\times 2$ matrix by repeated multiplication is tedious; for a diagonal matrix it is trivial, since $\operatorname{diag}(a, b)^{100} = \operatorname{diag}(a^{100}, b^{100})$. Diagonalisation is the art of making a matrix diagonal by choosing better coordinates.

The better coordinates are given by eigenvectors. If $A$ has a basis of [[eigen|eigenvectors]], then written in that basis $A$ simply multiplies each coordinate by its eigenvalue. This lesson makes that precise, shows how to use it, and pins down exactly when such a basis exists.

blocks.title: Diagonalisable matrix
blocks.body:
Let $F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. An $n \times n$ matrix $A$ with entries in $F$ is diagonalisable (over $F$) if there are an invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$, both with entries in $F$, such that
$$A = PDP^{-1}, \qquad \text{equivalently} \qquad P^{-1}AP = D.$$

In words: $A$ is similar to a diagonal matrix, that is, after a change of basis the map $x \mapsto Ax$ becomes coordinatewise multiplication.

blocks.title: Diagonalisation means an eigenbasis
blocks.body: $A = PDP^{-1}$ with $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$ if and only if the columns $p_1, \dots, p_n$ of $P$ form a basis of $F^n$ and $Ap_i = \lambda_i p_i$ for each $i$. So $A$ is diagonalisable exactly when $F^n$ has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.

$A = PDP^{-1}$ is the same as $AP = PD$ with $P$ invertible. The $i$-th column of $AP$ is $Ap_i$, and the $i$-th column of $PD$ is $\lambda_i p_i$, because multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the right scales the columns. So $AP = PD$ says exactly that $Ap_i = \lambda_i p_i$ for all $i$. Finally, an $n\times n$ matrix is invertible exactly when its columns form a basis of $F^n$.

blocks.title: Why it helps: powers and functions
blocks.body:
Once $A = PDP^{-1}$, all the $P$'s in the middle of a product cancel:
$$A^k = (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1})\cdots(PDP^{-1}) = PD^kP^{-1}, \qquad D^k = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k, \dots, \lambda_n^k).$$
The same holds for any polynomial, $q(A) = P\, q(D)\, P^{-1}$ with $q(D) = \operatorname{diag}(q(\lambda_1), \dots, q(\lambda_n))$, and, by taking limits of polynomials, for power series such as the matrix exponential
$$e^{tA} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{t^k A^k}{k!} = P \operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_1 t}, \dots, e^{\lambda_n t}) P^{-1}.$$
There is a cleaner way to say the same thing without matrices: write a vector in the eigenbasis, $x = c_1p_1 + \cdots + c_np_n$; then $A^kx = c_1\lambda_1^kp_1 + \cdots + c_n\lambda_n^kp_n$. The coordinates $c = P^{-1}x$ evolve independently. In particular, if $|\lambda_1|$ is strictly larger than the other $|\lambda_i|$ and $c_1 \ne 0$, then as $k$ grows the direction of $A^kx$ approaches the line through $p_1$, and $\|A^kx\|$ is of order $|\lambda_1|^k$.

From [[eigen]] we already know one sufficient condition: if $A$ has $n$ distinct eigenvalues, the corresponding eigenvectors are independent, hence a basis, and $A$ is diagonalisable. Repeated eigenvalues need more care.

blocks.title: What can go wrong
blocks.body:
The shear $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is the basic example of failure. Its only eigenvalue is $1$, with algebraic multiplicity $2$, and the eigenspace $\ker(S - I)$ is the line spanned by $(1, 0)$. There is no second independent eigenvector, so no eigenbasis. (If $S$ were $PDP^{-1}$, then $D$ would have both diagonal entries equal to $1$, so $D = I$ and $S = PIP^{-1} = I$, which is false.)

A different kind of failure is the rotation $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$: it has no real eigenvalues, so it is not diagonalisable over $\mathbb R$, but it has the distinct eigenvalues $\pm i$ and is diagonalisable over $\mathbb C$. So the field matters, and from now on we work over $\mathbb C$, where the characteristic polynomial always factors into linear factors.

For each eigenvalue $\lambda$ write $a_\lambda$ for its algebraic multiplicity (as a root of $p_A$) and $g_\lambda = \dim\ker(A - \lambda I)$ for its geometric multiplicity. For the shear $a_1 = 2$ and $g_1 = 1$.

blocks.title: The multiplicity criterion
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ complex matrix with distinct eigenvalues $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_s$.

1. For each eigenvalue, $1 \le g_\lambda \le a_\lambda$.
2. $A$ is diagonalisable if and only if $g_{\mu_j} = a_{\mu_j}$ for every $j$, that is, if and only if $g_{\mu_1} + \cdots + g_{\mu_s} = n$.

Part 1. Since $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, $g_\lambda \ge 1$. Let $g = g_\lambda$, choose a basis $v_1, \dots, v_g$ of $\ker(A - \lambda I)$ and extend it to a basis $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of $\mathbb C^n$ ([[basis-dimension]]). Let $P$ have these columns. Since $Av_i = \lambda v_i$ for $i \le g$, the first $g$ columns of $P^{-1}AP$ are $\lambda e_1, \dots, \lambda e_g$, so
$$P^{-1}AP = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda I_g & C\\ 0 & E \end{pmatrix}$$
for some blocks $C$, $E$. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, and $tI - P^{-1}AP$ has top-left block $(t - \lambda)I_g$ with only zeros below it; expanding $g$ times along the first column gives $p_A(t) = (t - \lambda)^g\, p_E(t)$. Hence $\lambda$ is a root of multiplicity at least $g$: $g_\lambda \le a_\lambda$.

Part 2. Since $p_A$ has degree $n$ and splits over $\mathbb C$, $\sum_j a_{\mu_j} = n$. By part 1, $\sum_j g_{\mu_j} = n$ holds exactly when every $g_{\mu_j} = a_{\mu_j}$.

If $A$ is diagonalisable, an eigenbasis contains, for each $j$, some number $m_j$ of independent vectors lying in $E_{\mu_j}$, so $m_j \le g_{\mu_j}$ and $n = \sum m_j \le \sum g_{\mu_j} \le \sum a_{\mu_j} = n$. Hence $\sum g_{\mu_j} = n$.

Conversely, suppose $\sum g_{\mu_j} = n$. Take a basis of each eigenspace $E_{\mu_j}$ and put them all together: $n$ vectors. They are independent. Indeed, group a linear relation among them by eigenvalue as $w_1 + \cdots + w_s = 0$ with $w_j \in E_{\mu_j}$. The nonzero $w_j$ would be eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues, which are independent by the theorem in [[eigen]], so no $w_j$ can be nonzero. Then each $w_j = 0$ is a relation among the basis vectors of $E_{\mu_j}$, so all its coefficients vanish. Thus we have $n$ independent eigenvectors, a basis of $\mathbb C^n$, and $A$ is diagonalisable.

blocks.title: A closed formula for powers
blocks.body: Diagonalise $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1\\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and find a formula for $A^n$.
blocks.solution:
In [[eigen]] we found the eigenvalues $5$ and $2$ with eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$. So
$$P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & -2\end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 0\\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}, \quad P^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix},$$
and $A = PDP^{-1}$. (The order of the columns of $P$ must match the order of the eigenvalues in $D$.) Multiplying out $PD^nP^{-1}$,
$$A^n = \frac13\begin{pmatrix} 2\cdot 5^n + 2^n & 5^n - 2^n\\ 2\cdot 5^n - 2\cdot 2^n & 5^n + 2\cdot 2^n\end{pmatrix}.$$
Check $n = 1$: the entries are $\frac{12}{3}, \frac33, \frac63, \frac93$, that is $4, 1, 2, 3$. For large $n$, $A^n \approx \frac{5^n}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$: the eigenvalue $5$ dominates and every column lines up with the eigenvector $(1,1)$.

blocks.title: A linear recurrence
blocks.body: The sequence $a_0 = 0$, $a_1 = 1$, $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + 2a_n$ begins $0, 1, 1, 3, 5, 11, 21, \dots$ Find a closed formula for $a_n$.
blocks.solution:
Put $x_n = (a_{n+1}, a_n)$. Then $x_{n+1} = Mx_n$ with $M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, so $x_n = M^n x_0$ and $x_0 = (1, 0)$.

$p_M(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \lambda - 2 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda + 1)$, with eigenvectors $(2, 1)$ for $2$ and $(-1, 1)$ for $-1$ (check: $M(2,1) = (4, 2)$ and $M(-1, 1) = (1, -1)$). Write the starting vector in the eigenbasis:
$$(1, 0) = \tfrac13 (2, 1) - \tfrac13(-1, 1).$$
Then $x_n = \frac13 2^n (2, 1) - \frac13 (-1)^n(-1, 1)$, and the second coordinate gives
$$a_n = \frac{2^n - (-1)^n}{3}.$$
Check: $a_5 = (32 + 1)/3 = 11$. The same method works for any linear recurrence with constant coefficients whose characteristic polynomial has distinct roots; repeated roots are where [[jordan|Jordan form]] enters.

blocks.title: Using the criterion
blocks.body:
Decide which of these matrices are diagonalisable:
$$B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}.$$
blocks.solution:
Both are upper triangular with diagonal $2, 2, 3$, so both have $p(t) = (t - 2)^2(t - 3)$: eigenvalue $2$ with $a_2 = 2$ and eigenvalue $3$ with $a_3 = 1$. For a simple eigenvalue $g = a = 1$ automatically, so everything depends on $g_2$.

For $B$: $B - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has rank $2$, so $g_2 = 3 - 2 = 1 < 2$. $B$ is not diagonalisable.

For $C$: $C - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so $g_2 = 2 = a_2$. $C$ is diagonalisable. Explicitly, $E_2$ is spanned by $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$, and solving $(C - 3I)v = 0$ gives $v = (1, 0, 1)$, so with $P$ having columns $(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,0,1)$ we get $P^{-1}CP = \operatorname{diag}(2, 2, 3)$.

Same eigenvalues, different answers: the characteristic polynomial alone cannot decide diagonalisability.

blocks.title: Projections
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a square matrix with $A^2 = A$ (a projection). Prove that $A$ is diagonalisable and that $\operatorname{tr} A = \operatorname{rank} A$.
blocks.solution:
Every vector splits as
$$v = Av + (v - Av).$$
The first part satisfies $A(Av) = A^2v = Av$, so it lies in $E_1 = \ker(A - I)$. The second satisfies $A(v - Av) = Av - A^2v = 0$, so it lies in $E_0 = \ker A$. Hence every vector is a sum of a vector of $E_1$ and a vector of $E_0$, so $\dim E_1 + \dim E_0 \ge n$. Bases of $E_1$ and $E_0$ together are independent (as in the proof of the criterion), so $\dim E_1 + \dim E_0 = n$ and these bases together form an eigenbasis. Thus $A = P\operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0)P^{-1}$ with $r = \dim E_1$ ones.

The trace is similarity invariant (it is a coefficient of $p_A$), so $\operatorname{tr}A = r$. And the image of $A$ is exactly $E_1$: every $Av$ lies in $E_1$, and every $u \in E_1$ equals $Au$. So $\operatorname{rank} A = \dim E_1 = r = \operatorname{tr} A$.

The same idea proves a general fact: if $q(A) = 0$ for some polynomial $q$ with distinct roots, then $A$ is diagonalisable. Here $q(t) = t^2 - t = t(t-1)$.

blocks.body:
- Diagonalisable and invertible are unrelated. The zero matrix is diagonal but not invertible; the shear $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible but not diagonalisable.
- The columns of $P$ must be listed in the same order as the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$. $P$ is not unique: each column can be rescaled, and within a repeated eigenvalue any basis of the eigenspace works.
- Repeated eigenvalues do not automatically prevent diagonalisation (the identity matrix has only the eigenvalue $1$). What matters is whether each eigenspace is as large as the multiplicity.
- A real matrix can be diagonalisable over $\mathbb C$ but not over $\mathbb R$; say which field you mean. A real matrix is diagonalisable over $\mathbb R$ exactly when all its eigenvalues are real and $g_\lambda = a_\lambda$ for each of them.
- $A = PDP^{-1}$ gives $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$, not $P^kD^kP^{-k}$.

Not every matrix is diagonalisable, and [[jordan|Jordan normal form]] describes what one can always achieve over $\mathbb C$ instead: a block diagonal matrix whose blocks have a single eigenvalue on the diagonal and $1$s just above it, with as many blocks as the maximal number of independent eigenvectors. For real symmetric matrices the situation is better than diagonalisable: the eigenbasis can be taken orthonormal, so $P^{-1} = P^{\mathsf T}$. That is [[spectral-theorem|the spectral theorem]].

The formula $e^{tA} = Pe^{tD}P^{-1}$ solves the system $x' = Ax$ of [[ode-linear|linear differential equations]], and $A^k = PD^kP^{-1}$ gives the $k$-step transition probabilities of a [[markov-chains|Markov chain]]. Closed formulas for recurrences like the one above are also obtained from [[generating-functions]], and solutions of [[pell|Pell's equation]] are generated by powers of a $2\times 2$ matrix whose eigenvalues are $x_1 \pm y_1\sqrt d$.

1. Diagonalise $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and compute its $n$-th power.
2. For which real numbers $c$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & c\\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ diagonalisable? For which $c$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & c\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$?
3. Find a matrix $B$ with $B^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4\\ 4 & 5\end{pmatrix}$.
4. Show that if $A$ is diagonalisable and its only eigenvalue is $\lambda$, then $A = \lambda I$.

entry.sum: An inner product $\langle u, v\rangle$ on a vector space generalises the dot product: it is linear in the first argument, symmetric (conjugate-symmetric over $\mathbb C$) and positive definite, and it defines lengths $\|v\| = \sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}$ and angles. Orthogonality, $\langle u, v\rangle = 0$, is the key notion: in an orthonormal basis coordinates are just inner products, and the closest point of a subspace is the orthogonal projection.
key: v=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle v,e_i\rangle\, e_i\quad\text{for an orthonormal basis } e_1,\dots,e_n
entry.why: Inner products bring Euclidean geometry (length, angle, perpendicularity, best approximation) into any vector space, including spaces of functions, which is the basis of least-squares fitting, Fourier series and the state spaces of quantum mechanics.

links.note: Fourier series expand a function in the orthonormal system $e^{2\pi i k x}$ with respect to $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 f\bar g$, and Parseval's identity is Pythagoras in infinitely many dimensions.
Quantum states are unit vectors in a complex inner product space, and the probability of a measurement outcome is $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^2$.

Covariance is an inner product on mean-zero random variables with finite variance (identifying variables that are equal with probability $1$), so correlation is the cosine of an angle and uncorrelated means orthogonal.

blocks.body:
In $\mathbb R^3$ the dot product $u \cdot v = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3$ gives lengths ($\|v\|^2 = v\cdot v$), angles ($u \cdot v = \|u\|\|v\|\cos\theta$) and the notion of perpendicular vectors ($u \cdot v = 0$). An abstract vector space has none of this: it knows how to add and scale, but not how long a vector is.

An inner product is the extra structure that supplies geometry. Once you have one, you can ask which polynomial of degree $1$ is closest to $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, or find coordinates without solving a linear system, using the same pictures as in the plane. This lesson builds that toolkit: the axioms, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, orthonormal bases, Gram–Schmidt, and orthogonal projection.

blocks.title: Inner product
Examples
blocks.body:
The standard examples:

- $\mathbb R^n$ with the dot product $\langle u, v\rangle = \sum u_iv_i = u^{\mathsf T}v$, and $\mathbb C^n$ with $\langle u, v\rangle = \sum u_i\overline{v_i}$. The conjugate is essential: without it, $\langle (1, i), (1, i)\rangle$ would be $1 + i^2 = 0$.
- Weighted versions $\sum c_iu_iv_i$ with all $c_i > 0$. Different inner products on the same space give different notions of perpendicular.
- Continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ with $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 f(x)g(x)\,dx$. Positivity holds because a continuous $f \ne 0$ has $f^2 > 0$ on some interval. Here $\langle 1, x - \frac12\rangle = 0$: the functions $1$ and $x - \frac12$ are orthogonal.
- Real $m\times n$ matrices with $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}B) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}b_{ij}$, the dot product of the matrices viewed as long vectors.

Expanding $\|u + v\|^2 = \langle u + v, u + v\rangle$ gives $\|u\|^2 + 2\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2$ in the real case. So Pythagoras holds: if $u \perp v$ then $\|u + v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2$ (over $\mathbb C$ the middle term is $2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle$, and the conclusion is the same).

blocks.title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
blocks.body:
For all $u, v$ in an inner product space,
$$|\langle u, v\rangle| \le \|u\|\,\|v\|,$$
with equality if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent. Consequently $\|u + v\| \le \|u\| + \|v\|$ (the triangle inequality).

If $v = 0$ both sides are $0$, and $u, v$ are dependent. Otherwise let $c = \langle u, v\rangle / \langle v, v\rangle$ and $w = u - cv$. This is the part of $u$ left after removing its component along $v$, and indeed
$$\langle w, v\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle - c\langle v, v\rangle = 0.$$
So $u = w + cv$ with $w \perp cv$, and Pythagoras gives
$$\|u\|^2 = \|w\|^2 + |c|^2\|v\|^2 \ge |c|^2\|v\|^2 = \frac{|\langle u, v\rangle|^2}{\|v\|^2}.$$
Multiplying by $\|v\|^2$ and taking square roots gives the inequality. Equality holds exactly when $w = 0$, that is $u = cv$; and if $u, v$ are dependent with $v \neq 0$, then $u$ is a multiple of $v$, which forces $u = cv$.

For the triangle inequality, $\|u + v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2 \le \|u\|^2 + 2\|u\|\|v\| + \|v\|^2 = (\|u\| + \|v\|)^2$.

blocks.title: Angles and orthonormal bases
blocks.body:
In a real inner product space, Cauchy–Schwarz says $-1 \le \frac{\langle u, v\rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|} \le 1$ for nonzero $u, v$, so we may define the angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ between them by $\cos\theta = \frac{\langle u, v\rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|}$. Applied to $\mathbb R^n$ it is the classical inequality $(\sum u_iv_i)^2 \le \sum u_i^2 \sum v_i^2$ of [[cauchy-schwarz]]; applied to functions it is $\left(\int fg\right)^2 \le \int f^2 \int g^2$.

A list $e_1, \dots, e_k$ is orthonormal if $\langle e_i, e_j\rangle = 0$ for $i \ne j$ and $\|e_i\| = 1$. Orthonormal lists are automatically independent: if $\sum c_ie_i = 0$, take the inner product with $e_j$ to get $c_j = 0$. The same computation shows why orthonormal bases are so convenient. If $v = \sum c_ie_i$, then
$$\langle v, e_j\rangle = \sum_i c_i\langle e_i, e_j\rangle = c_j,$$
so the coordinates are just inner products, with no linear system to solve:
$$v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \langle v, e_i\rangle e_i, \qquad \|v\|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n |\langle v, e_i\rangle|^2.$$
The second formula (Parseval's identity) is Pythagoras applied to the orthogonal pieces. In matrix language: a real square matrix $Q$ has orthonormal columns exactly when $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$, so its inverse is just its transpose. Such matrices are called orthogonal; they preserve inner products, $\langle Qx, Qy\rangle = x^{\mathsf T}Q^{\mathsf T}Qy = \langle x, y\rangle$, and hence lengths and angles. Rotations and reflections are examples.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt process
blocks.body:
Let $v_1, \dots, v_k$ be linearly independent vectors in an inner product space. Define recursively
$$u_j = v_j - \sum_{i < j} \langle v_j, e_i\rangle e_i, \qquad e_j = \frac{u_j}{\|u_j\|}.$$
Then $e_1, \dots, e_k$ is orthonormal and, for each $j$, $\operatorname{span}(e_1, \dots, e_j) = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \dots, v_j)$. In particular every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

Induction on $j$. Suppose $e_1, \dots, e_{j-1}$ are orthonormal with the same span as $v_1, \dots, v_{j-1}$. Then $u_j \ne 0$: otherwise $v_j$ would lie in $\operatorname{span}(e_1, \dots, e_{j-1}) = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \dots, v_{j-1})$, contradicting independence. So $e_j$ is defined and has norm $1$. For $l < j$,
$$\langle u_j, e_l\rangle = \langle v_j, e_l\rangle - \sum_{i<j}\langle v_j, e_i\rangle\langle e_i, e_l\rangle = \langle v_j, e_l\rangle - \langle v_j, e_l\rangle = 0,$$
so $e_j$ is orthogonal to the earlier vectors. Finally $e_j$ is a combination of $v_j$ and $e_1, \dots, e_{j-1}$, and $v_j$ is a combination of $e_j$ and $e_1, \dots, e_{j-1}$, so the spans agree. Applying the process to any basis ([[basis-dimension]]) gives an orthonormal basis.

blocks.title: Orthogonal projection and best approximation
blocks.body:
Let $W$ be a subspace with orthonormal basis $e_1, \dots, e_k$. The orthogonal complement is $W^\perp = \{v : \langle v, w\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}$, and the orthogonal projection onto $W$ is
$$P_Wv = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \langle v, e_i\rangle e_i.$$
Exactly as in the proof of Gram–Schmidt, $v - P_Wv$ is orthogonal to every $e_i$, hence lies in $W^\perp$. So every $v$ splits as $v = P_Wv + (v - P_Wv)$ with the first part in $W$ and the second in $W^\perp$. The split is unique, since a vector in both $W$ and $W^\perp$ is orthogonal to itself and so is $0$. This is the decomposition $V = W \oplus W^\perp$ in finite dimensions, and it gives $\dim W + \dim W^\perp = \dim V$.

The projection is the best approximation from $W$. For any $w \in W$, the vector $P_Wv - w$ lies in $W$ and $v - P_Wv$ lies in $W^\perp$, so by Pythagoras
$$\|v - w\|^2 = \|v - P_Wv\|^2 + \|P_Wv - w\|^2 \ge \|v - P_Wv\|^2,$$
with equality only for $w = P_Wv$. In practice you rarely need an orthonormal basis: $P_Wv$ is characterised by $v - P_Wv \perp w$ for every $w$ in a spanning set of $W$, which is a small linear system (the normal equations). This is the method of least squares.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt in R^3
blocks.body: Apply Gram–Schmidt to $v_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $v_2 = (1, 0, 1)$, $v_3 = (0, 1, 1)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with the dot product.
blocks.solution:
First $e_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1, 0)$.

Next $\langle v_2, e_1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $u_2 = v_2 - \frac12(1, 1, 0) = (\frac12, -\frac12, 1)$, with $\|u_2\|^2 = \frac14 + \frac14 + 1 = \frac32$. Rescaling, $e_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, -1, 2)$.

Finally $\langle v_3, e_1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\langle v_3, e_2\rangle = \frac{-1 + 2}{\sqrt 6} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}$, so
$$u_3 = (0, 1, 1) - \tfrac12(1, 1, 0) - \tfrac16(1, -1, 2) = \left(-\tfrac23, \tfrac23, \tfrac23\right), \qquad e_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1, 1, 1).$$
Check: $(1,1,0)\cdot(1,-1,2) = 0$, $(1,1,0)\cdot(-1,1,1) = 0$ and $(1,-1,2)\cdot(-1,1,1) = 0$. Now, for example, the coordinates of $x = (2, 0, 0)$ are $\langle x, e_i\rangle = \sqrt2, \frac{2}{\sqrt6}, -\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, and indeed $2 + \frac46 + \frac43 = 4 = \|x\|^2$.

blocks.title: Best linear approximation of a function
blocks.body: Find the polynomial $a + bx$ that minimises $\int_0^1 (x^2 - a - bx)^2\,dx$, and the minimum value.
blocks.solution:
Work in continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ with $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 fg$. We want the projection of $x^2$ onto $W = \operatorname{span}(1, x)$, characterised by $x^2 - a - bx \perp 1$ and $\perp x$. Using $\int_0^1 x^k\,dx = \frac{1}{k+1}$:
$$\tfrac13 - a - \tfrac12 b = 0, \qquad \tfrac14 - \tfrac12 a - \tfrac13 b = 0.$$
From the first, $a = \frac13 - \frac b2$; substituting, $\frac14 - \frac16 + \frac b4 - \frac b3 = 0$, i.e. $\frac{1}{12} - \frac{b}{12} = 0$. So $b = 1$, $a = -\frac16$, and the best approximation is $x - \frac16$.

The error is $r(x) = x^2 - x + \frac16$, and since $r \perp W$, $\|r\|^2 = \langle r, x^2\rangle = \frac15 - \frac14 + \frac1{18} = \frac{1}{180}$. Note that the answer is neither the chord $y = x$ nor any tangent line of $y = x^2$; it is the best fit in the averaged, squared sense.

blocks.title: Pairwise obtuse vectors
blocks.body: Vectors $v_1, \dots, v_m \in \mathbb R^n$ satisfy $\langle v_i, v_j\rangle < 0$ for all $i \ne j$. Prove that $m \le n + 1$, and show that $m = n + 1$ is possible.
blocks.solution:
We show that $v_1, \dots, v_{m-1}$ are linearly independent; then $m - 1 \le n$.

Suppose $\sum_{i < m} c_iv_i = 0$. Move the terms with negative coefficients to the other side: with $P = \{i : c_i > 0\}$ and $N = \{i : c_i < 0\}$,
$$w := \sum_{i \in P} c_iv_i = \sum_{j \in N} (-c_j)v_j.$$
Taking the inner product of the two expressions for $w$,
$$\|w\|^2 = \sum_{i\in P}\sum_{j \in N} c_i(-c_j)\langle v_i, v_j\rangle \le 0,$$
because every coefficient $c_i(-c_j)$ is positive and every $\langle v_i, v_j\rangle$ is negative (and $P \cap N = \varnothing$). So $w = 0$. If $P$ were nonempty, then
$$0 = \langle w, v_m\rangle = \sum_{i \in P} c_i\langle v_i, v_m\rangle < 0,$$
a contradiction; so $P = \varnothing$, and likewise (using the second expression for $w$) $N = \varnothing$. All $c_i$ are $0$.

For $m = n + 1$, take the vertices of a regular simplex centred at the origin: in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ let $u_i = e_i - \frac{1}{n+1}(1, \dots, 1)$ for $i = 1, \dots, n+1$. Then $\langle u_i, u_j\rangle = -\frac{1}{n+1}$ for $i \ne j$, and all $u_i$ lie in the $n$-dimensional subspace $x_1 + \cdots + x_{n+1} = 0$, which is a copy of $\mathbb R^n$ (choose an orthonormal basis of it). For $n = 2$ these are three vectors in a plane at $120^\circ$ to each other.

blocks.body:
- Over $\mathbb C$, forgetting the conjugate breaks positivity. Also, books differ on which slot is linear: here it is the first, while physics texts usually make the second slot linear. Formulas such as $P_Wv = \sum\langle v, e_i\rangle e_i$ must then be rewritten as $\sum \langle e_i, v\rangle e_i$.
- An orthogonal matrix has orthonormal columns, not merely orthogonal ones: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has orthogonal columns but does not satisfy $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$.
- The formula $P_Wv = \sum \langle v, w_i\rangle w_i$ is valid only for an orthonormal basis $w_i$ of $W$; with a merely spanning or non-normalised set, solve the normal equations instead.
- Orthogonality depends on the inner product. $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ are orthogonal for the dot product but not for $\langle u, v\rangle = 2u_1v_1 + u_2v_2$.
- Gram–Schmidt depends on the order of the input vectors; different orders give different orthonormal bases of the same space.

The main theorem built on inner products is [[spectral-theorem|the spectral theorem]]: a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. It in turn yields [[svd|the singular value decomposition]], which describes any matrix by two orthonormal bases. In matrix form, Gram–Schmidt is the factorisation $A = QR$ with $Q$ having orthonormal columns and $R$ upper triangular, which, computed in a numerically stable way, is a standard tool for least-squares problems arising from [[linear-systems]] with more equations than unknowns.

With $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 f\overline{g}$, the functions $e^{2\pi i kx}$ are orthonormal, and expanding in them is Fourier series ([[fourier-poisson]]). Infinite-dimensional complete inner product spaces (Hilbert spaces) need the ideas of [[metric-spaces]] and [[lebesgue|the Lebesgue integral]]. In probability, $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$ is an inner product on mean-zero [[random-variables]] with finite variance (identifying variables that are equal with probability $1$), and the coordinate geometry of [[analytic-geometry]] is the dot product in $\mathbb R^2$ and $\mathbb R^3$.

1. Find an orthonormal basis of the plane $x + y + z = 0$ in $\mathbb R^3$, and the projection of $(1, 2, 6)$ onto it.
2. Show that $\langle p, q\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2)$ is an inner product on polynomials of degree at most $2$, but not on polynomials of degree at most $3$.
3. Prove the parallelogram law $\|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2$.
4. Show that $W^\perp$ is a subspace and that $(W^\perp)^\perp = W$ when $V$ is finite-dimensional.

entry.sum: The spectral theorem says that every real symmetric matrix $A$ can be diagonalised by an orthogonal change of basis: $A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal. Equivalently, its eigenvalues are real and it has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so the map $x\mapsto Ax$ is a stretch along perpendicular axes; the same holds for complex Hermitian matrices with a unitary $Q$.
key: A=A^{\mathsf T}\ \Longrightarrow\ A=QDQ^{\mathsf T},\qquad Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I,\ D\ \text{real diagonal}
entry.why: Symmetric and Hermitian matrices are everywhere (Hessians, covariance matrices, adjacency matrices of graphs, quantum observables), and the spectral theorem reduces each of them to independent one-dimensional pieces: principal axes of a conic, principal components of data, normal modes of a vibrating system.

links.note: The second-derivative test in several variables diagonalises the symmetric Hessian matrix: a critical point is a local minimum when all its eigenvalues are positive.
A covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, and its orthonormal eigenvectors are the principal components used in principal component analysis.

Observables in quantum mechanics are self-adjoint operators whose real eigenvalues are the possible measurement results, and the principal axes of inertia of a rigid body are the eigenvectors of its inertia tensor.

blocks.body:
What does the curve $5x^2 + 4xy + 2y^2 = 1$ look like? The cross term $4xy$ hides the answer. If we could rotate the coordinate axes so that the cross term disappears, we would see an ellipse with its axes along the new coordinate directions. The spectral theorem says that such a rotation always exists, for any number of variables, and that the right axes are the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix.

General matrices can fail to be diagonalisable, or have complex eigenvalues, or have eigenvectors at awkward angles. Symmetric matrices have none of these problems: their eigenvalues are real and their eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular. This lesson proves that, using [[diagonalization]] and [[inner-products]], and shows what it buys.

blocks.title: Symmetric and self-adjoint
blocks.body:
A real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is symmetric if $A^{\mathsf T} = A$, that is $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$. With the dot product $\langle x, y\rangle = x^{\mathsf T}y$ this is equivalent to
$$\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \mathbb R^n,$$
since $\langle Ax, y\rangle = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y$. A linear map with this property on an inner product space is called self-adjoint. A complex matrix with $\overline{A}^{\mathsf T} = A$ is called Hermitian; it is self-adjoint for $\langle x, y\rangle = \sum x_i\overline{y_i}$.

So a symmetric matrix is one that can be moved from one side of the inner product to the other.

blocks.title: The spectral theorem
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix. Then all eigenvalues of $A$ are real, and $\mathbb R^n$ has an orthonormal basis $q_1, \dots, q_n$ of eigenvectors of $A$. Equivalently, there are an orthogonal matrix $Q$ (with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$) and a real diagonal matrix $D$ with
$$A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}.$$
Conversely, every matrix of the form $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal is symmetric. The analogous statement holds for complex Hermitian matrices, with $Q$ unitary ($\overline{Q}^{\mathsf T}Q = I$) and $D$ still real.

blocks.title: Two key facts
blocks.body:
The proof rests on two short observations.

Eigenvalues are real. Let $Av = \lambda v$ with $v \in \mathbb C^n$ nonzero (over $\mathbb C$ an eigenvalue always exists). Write $v^* = \overline{v}^{\mathsf T}$ and consider the number $s = v^*Av$. On the one hand $s = \lambda\, v^*v = \lambda\sum|v_i|^2$. On the other hand, since $A$ is real and symmetric, $\overline{s} = v^{\mathsf T}A\overline{v}$, and this $1\times 1$ matrix equals its own transpose $\overline{v}^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}v = v^*Av = s$. So $s$ is real, and $\lambda = s/\sum|v_i|^2$ is real. Then $A - \lambda I$ is a real singular matrix, so it also has a nonzero real vector in its kernel: real eigenvalues have real eigenvectors.

Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular. If $Av = \lambda v$ and $Aw = \mu w$ with $\lambda \ne \mu$, then
$$\lambda\langle v, w\rangle = \langle Av, w\rangle = \langle v, Aw\rangle = \mu\langle v, w\rangle,$$
so $(\lambda - \mu)\langle v, w\rangle = 0$ and $\langle v, w\rangle = 0$.

These two facts already prove the theorem when the eigenvalues are distinct: normalise one eigenvector for each eigenvalue. Repeated eigenvalues need an extra argument, because we must also show that each eigenspace is as large as the multiplicity. That is done by induction.

Proof of the spectral theorem. Induction on $n$; for $n = 1$ there is nothing to prove. Let $n \ge 2$. By the first key fact, $A$ has a real eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ with a real eigenvector, which we normalise to a unit vector $q_1$.

Let $W = q_1^{\perp} = \{w : \langle w, q_1\rangle = 0\}$, a subspace of dimension $n - 1$. The map $x \mapsto Ax$ sends $W$ into itself: if $w \in W$ then
$$\langle Aw, q_1\rangle = \langle w, Aq_1\rangle = \lambda_1\langle w, q_1\rangle = 0.$$
Choose an orthonormal basis $f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}$ of $W$ (Gram–Schmidt, see [[inner-products]]). The matrix $B$ of $A$ restricted to $W$ in this basis has entries $b_{ij} = \langle Af_j, f_i\rangle$, because coordinates in an orthonormal basis are inner products. Since $A$ is self-adjoint, $b_{ij} = \langle f_j, Af_i\rangle = b_{ji}$, so $B$ is a real symmetric $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix.

By the induction hypothesis, $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of $B$. Translating coordinates back through $f_1, \dots, f_{n-1}$ (which preserves inner products), $W$ has an orthonormal basis $q_2, \dots, q_n$ of eigenvectors of $A$. Each of these is orthogonal to $q_1$, so $q_1, \dots, q_n$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.

Finally let $Q$ have columns $q_1, \dots, q_n$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)$. Then $AQ = QD$ (column by column) and $Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$ (orthonormality), so $A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. The converse is the computation $(QDQ^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T} = QD^{\mathsf T}Q^{\mathsf T} = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. The Hermitian case is the same proof with $\overline{\,\cdot\,}^{\mathsf T}$ in place of ${}^{\mathsf T}$.

blocks.title: Principal axes and quadratic forms
blocks.body:
Multiplying out $QDQ^{\mathsf T}$ column by row gives the spectral decomposition
$$A = \lambda_1q_1q_1^{\mathsf T} + \lambda_2q_2q_2^{\mathsf T} + \cdots + \lambda_nq_nq_n^{\mathsf T}.$$
Each $q_iq_i^{\mathsf T}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line through $q_i$ (it sends $x$ to $\langle x, q_i\rangle q_i$). So a symmetric matrix is a weighted sum of projections onto perpendicular lines: decompose $x$ along the axes $q_i$, stretch the $i$-th piece by $\lambda_i$, and add up. The unit sphere is mapped to an ellipsoid (flattened if some $\lambda_i = 0$) whose semi-axes point along the $q_i$ and have lengths $|\lambda_i|$.

The same decomposition simplifies quadratic forms. In the coordinates $y = Q^{\mathsf T}x$ (a rotation, possibly composed with a reflection),
$$x^{\mathsf T}Ax = x^{\mathsf T}QDQ^{\mathsf T}x = y^{\mathsf T}Dy = \lambda_1y_1^2 + \cdots + \lambda_ny_n^2,$$
and $\|y\| = \|x\|$. Two consequences follow at once.

- $A$ is positive definite ($x^{\mathsf T}Ax > 0$ for all $x \ne 0$) if and only if all its eigenvalues are positive.
- Rayleigh's principle: on the unit sphere, $x^{\mathsf T}Ax = \sum\lambda_iy_i^2$ with $\sum y_i^2 = 1$ is a weighted average of the eigenvalues. Hence
$$\lambda_{\min} \le x^{\mathsf T}Ax \le \lambda_{\max} \quad \text{for } \|x\| = 1,$$
with the maximum attained at a unit eigenvector for $\lambda_{\max}$ and the minimum at one for $\lambda_{\min}$.

blocks.title: Orthogonal diagonalisation with a repeated eigenvalue
blocks.body:
Find an orthogonal matrix $Q$ with $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ$ diagonal, where
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.$$
blocks.solution:
$A = I + J$ with $J$ the all-ones matrix, so (see [[eigen]]) the eigenvalues are $4$, with eigenvector $(1, 1, 1)$, and $1$, with eigenspace the plane $x + y + z = 0$.

The unit vector $q_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)$ handles $\lambda = 4$. For $\lambda = 1$, any two independent vectors in the plane are eigenvectors, but they need not be orthogonal: $(1, -1, 0)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$ have inner product $1$. Apply Gram–Schmidt inside the eigenspace: $q_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$, then
$$(1, 0, -1) - \tfrac12(1, -1, 0) = \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, -1\right), \qquad q_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2).$$
With $Q = (q_1\ q_2\ q_3)$ we get $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1, 1)$. The key point: eigenvectors for different eigenvalues came out orthogonal for free; within a repeated eigenvalue we had to orthogonalise by hand.

blocks.title: Principal axes of a conic
blocks.body: Identify the curve $5x^2 + 4xy + 2y^2 = 1$.
blocks.solution:
Write the left side as $x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ with $x = (x, y)$ and
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2\\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$$
(the cross coefficient $4$ is split equally between the two off-diagonal entries so that $A$ is symmetric). Here $\operatorname{tr} A = 7$ and $\det A = 6$, so the eigenvalues are $6$ and $1$. Solving $(A - 6I)v = 0$ gives $v = (2, 1)$; solving $(A - I)v = 0$ gives $v = (1, -2)$. These are orthogonal, as they must be.

In the rotated coordinates $u = \frac{2x + y}{\sqrt5}$, $w = \frac{x - 2y}{\sqrt5}$ the equation becomes
$$6u^2 + w^2 = 1,$$
an ellipse with semi-axis $\frac{1}{\sqrt6}$ in the direction $(2, 1)$ and semi-axis $1$ in the direction $(1, -2)$. Its area is $\pi\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\cdot 1 = \pi/\sqrt{\det A}$.

blocks.title: An inequality from the Rayleigh principle
blocks.body: Find the largest and smallest values of $xy + yz + zx$ over all real $x, y, z$ with $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$.
blocks.solution:
We have $xy + yz + zx = v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ for $v = (x, y, z)$ and
$$M = \frac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac12(J - I).$$
$J$ has eigenvalues $3, 0, 0$, so $M$ has eigenvalues $\frac{3-1}{2} = 1$ and $\frac{0-1}{2} = -\frac12$ (twice). By Rayleigh's principle the maximum is $1$, attained at $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1)$, and the minimum is $-\frac12$, attained at any unit vector with $x + y + z = 0$, for instance $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$.

Equivalently, for all real $x, y, z$,
$$-\tfrac12(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) \le xy + yz + zx \le x^2 + y^2 + z^2.$$
Both are classical olympiad inequalities, usually proved from $(x - y)^2 + (y - z)^2 + (z - x)^2 \ge 0$ and $(x + y + z)^2 \ge 0$. The eigenvalue method explains where these sums of squares come from and why the constants are sharp.

blocks.title: Symmetric roots of the identity
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a real symmetric matrix with $A^k = I$ for some $k \ge 1$. Prove that $A^2 = I$.
blocks.solution:
Write $A = QDQ^{\mathsf T}$. Then $A^k = QD^kQ^{\mathsf T} = I$ gives $D^k = Q^{\mathsf T}Q = I$, so every eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda^k = 1$. The eigenvalues are real, and the only real $k$-th roots of unity are $\pm1$, so $\lambda^2 = 1$ for every eigenvalue. Hence $D^2 = I$ and $A^2 = QD^2Q^{\mathsf T} = QQ^{\mathsf T} = I$.

Without symmetry this fails: the rotation by $120^\circ$ satisfies $R^3 = I$ but $R^2 \ne I$. Its eigenvalues $e^{\pm 2\pi i/3}$ are not real, and that is exactly what the spectral theorem rules out.

blocks.body:
- The theorem needs symmetry, not just real eigenvalues. $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has real eigenvalues $1, 2$ and is diagonalisable, but its eigenvectors $(1, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$ are not perpendicular, so no orthogonal $Q$ works.
- Over $\mathbb C$ the right condition is Hermitian, not symmetric. The complex symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i\\ i & -1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2 = 0$ with $A \ne 0$, so it is not diagonalisable at all. More generally, a complex matrix $A$ can be written $A = UDU^{-1}$ with $U$ unitary and $D$ diagonal (now possibly with non-real entries) if and only if it is normal, $A\overline{A}^{\mathsf T} = \overline{A}^{\mathsf T}A$; we do not prove this here. Hermitian, real orthogonal and unitary matrices are normal.
- Eigenvectors for a repeated eigenvalue are not automatically orthogonal; orthogonalise inside each eigenspace.
- In a quadratic form $ax^2 + bxy + cy^2$, the symmetric matrix has off-diagonal entries $b/2$, not $b$.
- $Q^{\mathsf T}AQ$ is diagonal; $QAQ^{\mathsf T}$ in general is not. Keep track of which way the change of basis goes.

Applying the spectral theorem to the symmetric matrix $A^{\mathsf T}A$ of an arbitrary matrix $A$ gives [[svd|the singular value decomposition]]. In several-variable calculus, the second-derivative test classifies a critical point by the eigenvalues of the symmetric Hessian matrix of [[partial-derivatives]], and maximising $x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ on the unit sphere is the model case of [[lagrange-multipliers]]: the multiplier is the eigenvalue.

Integer-valued versions of quadratic forms are the subject of [[quadratic-forms]], where orthogonal changes of variable are replaced by integer ones. The adjacency matrix of a graph is symmetric, and its eigenvalues bound the chromatic number and measure expansion ([[graph-basics]], [[graph-coloring]]). Random Hermitian matrices, and the spacings between their real eigenvalues, are the model behind [[pair-correlation]] for zeros of the zeta function. Infinite-dimensional versions, for self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces, underlie Fourier analysis ([[fourier-poisson]]) and quantum mechanics.

1. Orthogonally diagonalise $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4\\ 4 & -3\end{pmatrix}$ and describe the map geometrically.
